blocks.text: Ἐκ δ᾽ ἀγγέων ἐλάσειας ἀράχνια [Ek d᾽ angeōn elaseias arachnia], [II, 512] But you will drive the spiders out of the vessels, that is, emptiness and want. Accordingly the Scholiast explains it thus: Εἰ καλῶς ἀροτριάσεις, καὶ σπείρεις, ἁδροὺς ἕξεις στάχους (lege στάχυας). Ἐκ δὲ τῶν σιτοφόρων σου κιβωτίων τῶν μέχρι τότε κενῶν ἑστηκότων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀραχνιέντων, ἐξελάσειας τὰ ἀράχνια, καὶ ἐμπλήσεις δηλονότι ταῦτα τοῦ σίτου [Ei kalōs arotriaseis, kai speireis, hadrous hexeis stachous (lege stachyas). Ek de tōn sitophorōn sou kibōtiōn tōn mechri tote kenōn hestēkotōn, kai dia touto arachnientōn, exelaseias ta arachnia, kai emplēseis dēlonoti tauta tou sitou]; If you plough and sow well, you will have thick ears of grain; and from your grain vessels, which until then had been empty and therefore full of spiders, you will drive out the spiders, namely so that you may fill them with grain. Therefore it is hardly likely that Solomon assigned spiders a home in the palaces of kings.

What, then, will שממית semamith be? Plainly another animal, namely the stellio. This is proved by so many arguments that learned men weary themselves in vain seeking another interpretation, since this one is true and certain, and fits the passage best. As its authorities I have, first, the LXX translators, for whom שממית semamith is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], the stellio. For Mercerus, following the Complutensians, is mistaken in asserting that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] there is a kind of fish. Καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is indeed among the fishes, but also among the lizards. Both are in Hesychius: Καλαβώτης· ἰχθῦς ποῖος, καὶ σαῦρος [Kalabōtēs; ichthys poios, kai sauros]. Clearly καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is the same as ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs]. Hence at Levit. XI, 30. the Complutensian and Parisian editions have καλαβώτην [kalabōtēn] for the Hebrew הלטאה, where the others have ἀσκαλαβώτην [askalabōtēn]. Nor should anyone believe that the Greeks were so mad as to count a fish among ἐν ἐλαχίστοις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [en elachistois epi tēs gēs]. 2. To the Greeks I add Jerome, in whom שממית semamith here is the stellio. 3. Also the Syriac translator, for whom ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, is the very same thing, as we proved abundantly above ^{b)} in the chapter on אנקה anaka. 4. As also the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, with the order of the letters changed, as in forma [form] from μόρφη [morphē].

Moreover, that very word שממית semamith, for a kind of lizard, and indeed for the stellio, is known to us from elsewhere as well. For at Lev. XI, 30. one reads [?] or [?] semamitha in the Samaritan translator and in the two Chaldee ones, Jonathan and the other, named after the city: in the former for אנקה anaka, in the latter for לטאה letaa, where the Greek version has καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] and the Roman stellio. Finally, that the ancient Hebrews used it in this way is evident from what is read in the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 8, p. 77b: אימת שממית על העקרב, The terror of the semamith is upon the scorpion. By these words they indicate that this animal is a terror to the scorpion. Hence it appears that the semamith is not the spider. For no one has written that it carries on enmity with the scorpion or is a terror to it. But concerning the scorpion Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, says thus: The stellio is reported to be especially hostile to scorpions, so that even by its sight it brings them fear and a torpor of cold sweat. And Aelian, History [II, 513] book 6, chapter 22: Ἔχθιστα δὲ τῷ μὲν λέοντι πῦρ, καὶ ἀλεκτρυών· ὕαινα δὲ τῇ παρδάλει· σκορπίος δὲ ἀσκαλαβώτῃ, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει προαχθέντος οἱ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ προειρημένου [Echthista de tō men leonti pyr, kai alektryōn; hyaina de tē pardalei; skorpios de askalabōtē, narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei proachthentos hoi tou zōou tou proeirēmenou]; Most hostile to the lion are fire and the cock; the hyena to the panther; and the scorpion to the stellio, at whose approach it is seized with torpor. And Galen, On Theriac, to Piso, book 1, chapter 9: Ὁ οὖν ἀσκαλαβώτης, ὁραθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν σκορπίων, πήγνυσιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὕτως ἀναιρεῖ [Ho oun askalabōtēs, horatheis hypo tōn skorpiōn, pēgnysin autous, kai houtōs anairei]; The stellio, when seen by scorpions, stupefies them and so kills them. And Isidore, book 12, chapter 4: The stellio is reported to be so hostile to scorpions that, when it is seen, it brings them fear and terror. And Phile, chapter 29, from Aelian, wrongly read and understood:
— — — ἡ δ᾽ ὕαινα πάρδαλιν, Καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην ὁ φθορεὺς κλὼψ σκορπίος, Νάρκη δὲ τοῦτον· — — — — — [hē d᾽ hyaina pardalin, Kai askalabōtēn ho phthoreus klōps skorpios, Narkē de touton]
